Highlights:
Codebase Diagram Generator: Visualize Your Architecture with AI

# Codebase Architecture Diagram Generator

Your code already knows the architecture. Paste what encodes it or connect the repository, and the AI draws a system-level diagram you can edit, export, and keep in sync.

Try: Draw the architecture of this codebase: React SPA, Rails API, Sidekiq workers, Postgres, Redis, S3 uploads Here is my docker-compose and my services folder listing, draw the system and label the data flows Monorepo with apps/web, apps/api, packages/shared, infra/terraform, draw how the deployed pieces connect From this Kubernetes manifests folder, draw the deployments, services, and ingress as an architecture diagram

...

How does a codebase become an architecture diagram?▼

The AI reads what encodes the system rather than parsing every import: compose files, IaC, CI config, folder structure, service entry points. From that it draws a system-level picture of what runs, what talks to what, and where state lives, on a canvas you can edit and refine with follow-up instructions.

How do I keep the diagram in sync with the code?▼

Connect the repository through the repo sync feature. Datadef supports GitHub, GitLab, and Azure DevOps cloud repos, connected with a public URL or a read-only token, one branch or tag per diagram. A daily sync re-reads the code and regenerates the diagram, with manual refresh and MCP tools when you want it now, and the generated architecture doc embeds the live diagram when it is public. This is part of Pro and Team, and a sync regenerates only when the repository actually changed.

Is this a UML or class diagram tool?▼

No. The output is system architecture: services, databases, queues, third-party APIs, and the connections between them. For class-level structure or call graphs, a static-analysis tool tied to your language is the better fit.

Can my coding agent draw the diagram instead?▼

Yes. Datadef ships an MCP server, so Claude Code, Cursor, or any MCP client with your repository open can drive the canvas directly and draw what it finds, using its full context of the code.

# Codebase Mermaid Generator

Generate Mermaid diagrams of your codebase structure directly within Visual Studio Code using the power of Anthropic's AI models.

## Features

- Analyzes the code within your current workspace.
- Uses the Anthropic API (Claude models) to understand code structure and relationships.

## Requirements

1. Ensure API Key is Set: Make sure you have added your Anthropic API key to the extension settings (see above).

## 🚀 Features

- 👀 **Instant Visualization**: Convert any GitHub repository structure into a system design / architecture diagram
- 🎨 **Interactivity**: Click on components to navigate directly to source files and relevant directories
- ⚡ **Fast Generation**: Powered by GPT-5-family models, with OpenAI for user-supplied browser keys and optional self-hosted providers such as OpenRouter or Atlas Cloud
- 🖼️ **Export Options**: Copy Mermaid code or download the generated diagram as PNG

...

Given any public (or private!) GitHub repository it generates diagrams in Mermaid.js with GPT-5-family models. The default setup uses GPT-5.4 mini through OpenAI, while self-hosted operators can optionally point the backend at OpenRouter or Atlas Cloud via environment configuration.

## ⚙️ How GitDiagram Works

When you submit a GitHub repo URL, GitDiagram asks the GitHub API for the repo's default branch, a recursive file tree, and the README, while filtering out noisy assets and dependency folders. It feeds that repo snapshot into a streamed generation pipeline where one model pass writes a plain-English architecture explanation and a second pass turns that explanation plus the file tree into a structured graph of systems, nodes, edges, and real repo paths.

That graph is validated against the actual file tree, retried with feedback if it contains bad paths or invalid connections, then compiled into Mermaid and validated again before it is shown. Any node tied to a real path becomes clickable back to GitHub, and the final explanation, graph, diagram, and terminal generation state are stored in Cloudflare R2 and Upstash Redis so the app can reopen an existing result or show where a run failed.

# Cartographer

Generate architecture documentation from codebases. Point at any repo, get a map.

## Why?

Every codebase has documentation that was accurate two years ago, scattered comments, and tribal knowledge locked in the heads of developers who've already left. New developers spend weeks figuring out where things are.

Cartographer reads your code and generates living documentation - architecture diagrams, module explanations, dependency graphs. Documentation that can't drift because it's derived from source.

## Features

- **Multi-language support**: Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Rust, Go, Java, C, C++
- **LLM explanations**: Generate natural language descriptions of modules and classes (Ollama, OpenAI)
- **React component detection**: Automatically identifies React functional components
- **Rust support**: Parses structs, enums, traits, impl blocks, use statements
- **Go support**: Parses packages, structs, interfaces, methods, imports
- **Dependency graphs**: See what imports what, find circular dependencies
- **Module detection**: Group files into logical components
- **Beautiful output**: Static HTML site you can deploy anywhere
- **Metrics**: Lines of code, class count, import statistics

## Quick Start

```bash
# Install
cargo install cartographer

# Analyze a project (Python, JS, or TS)
cartographer analyze ./my-project

# Serve the generated docs
cartographer serve ./cartographer-docs
```

## Usage

```
cartographer analyze <path> [options]

Options:
  -o, --output <dir>     Output directory (default: ./cartographer-docs)
  --exclude <patterns>   Glob patterns to exclude (repeatable)
  --include <patterns>   Glob patterns to include
  -c, --config <file>    Config file path (default: cartographer.toml)
  --format <type>        Output format: html, json, markdown
  --depth <n>            Max dependency depth (default: 5)
  --no-diagrams          Skip diagram generation
  --no-explain           Skip LLM-generated explanations
  -v, --verbose          Verbose output
```
